subject: Post-call: SDK / Auth / Routing questions (Chat vs Completions, streaming, embeddings)
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Alex Rivera <alex.r@acmeanalytics.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 01 Mar 2026 09:18:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call recap + next steps (SDK auth, routing, streaming semantics)

Hi Alex / Bethany —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and agreed next steps so we have a written reference for the technical team: 

Summary from our discovery
- Primary use case: multi-tenant analytics assistant for customers to query their data and get structured results (tables + JSON) + links to source docs.
- Volume: pilot ~50k requests/day, production target 400–600k/day within 6 months.
- SLOs: 95th pct latency target ~350ms on short queries; some long-run queries can be async.

Key technical topics to address (you flagged these):
1) SDK setup & auth: short lived API keys vs OAuth for end-user context, and server-side routing of requests.
2) Routing & fallbacks: preference for hosted model with dedicated fallbacks for private data lanes.
3) Structured output & tool-calling: deterministic schema for table output + safe tool invocation for lookups.
4) Chat vs completions semantics: how to choose request/response schema, token budgeting, stop sequences.
5) Streaming semantics & partial results: support for SSE/Websocket streaming and how it affects token accounting.
6) Embeddings + reranker: retrieval pipeline recommendations for recall vs reranking cost.

Deliverables I promised:
- Quickstart SDK doc (attached) and a short example payload for Chat vs Completion.
- Engineering note from Dev on auth/routing + streaming semantics (copied Dev & Karthik).
- Proposed follow-up: 30–45m technical deep-dive next Wed or Thu.

Action items / owners
- Alex: share any compliance or CORS constraints for the browser agent (Bethany) — due Tue 3/2.
- Dev: write architecture note with example request/response and token calc — due Wed 3/3.
- Marissa: schedule deep-dive once we have Dev's note.

Attachments: redwood_sdk_quickstart.pdf (SDK quickstart + examples), mutual_action_plan.xlsx

Thanks — talk soon,

—Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: Alex Rivera <alex.r@acmeanalytics.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Bethany Nguyen <bethany.nguyen@acmeanalytics.com>
Date: Mon, 01 Mar 2026 11:03:22 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call recap + next steps (SDK auth, routing, streaming semantics)

Marissa — thanks for the recap. A couple clarifying questions from our engineering side before the deep-dive: 

1) Auth model: we expect to issue tokens on behalf of our end-users in the browser; can the Redwood SDK do delegated auth (we would mint short-lived tokens tied to a user-id) and still allow server-side routing for billing/controls? Any example flows?

2) Structured output: we need a guaranteed JSON table for programmatic ingestion (rows + typed columns). Does Redwood support schema enforcement or tool-calling to populate a table object reliably? What happens if the model hallucinated an extra column?

3) Chat vs completions: we have two paths — short Q&A where a single completion suffices, and multi-turn diagnostic conversations. How do we decide between the chat API and completion-style payloads? Are tokens counted differently?

4) Streaming: if we stream partial results to the client (we want progressive UI), can we get partial structured output (e.g., first chunk contains first N rows) or is structured output only available once generation completes? Also what are the semantics for stop sequences in streaming?

If Dev or Karthik can draft a short note with examples (including a sample request body for chat vs completion and a note on tokenization/max_tokens) that would help our infra folks. Happy to carve out time Wed morning for the deep-dive.

—Alex
Senior Eng Manager, Acme Analytics

From: Dev Patel <dev@redwood.com>
To: Alex Rivera <alex.r@acmeanalytics.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 02 Mar 2026 10:42:11 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call recap + next steps (SDK auth, routing, streaming semantics)

Alex — quick engineering note below with concrete examples. Happy to expand in the deep-dive.

1) Auth / SDK flows-
- Recommended pattern: browser gets a short-lived session token from your backend (opaque or JWT) that your backend exchanges/validates and mints a Redwood short-lived API key scoped to the user/session. This lets Redwood enforce billing & routing at request-time while preserving end-user identity.
- We support API key auth (server-to-server) and delegated tokens via our token-exchange endpoint. Example flow:

  1. User authenticates to Acme; Acme backend issues session cookie + user-id.
  2. Acme backend calls Redwood /v1/tokens/exchange with backend credentials to create a short-lived key scoped: {scope: ["inference:chat"], user_id: "acme:u-12345", expires_in: 900}.
  3. Browser uses that short-lived key with the Redwood JS SDK to call chat/completions; Redwood ties usage to your account and user_id metadata.

- Important: never embed long-lived Redwood API keys in the browser.

2) Routing & fallbacks-
- You can set a routing policy per request header or tenant metadata: preferred_model, region, fallback_model. Example header: X-Redwood-Routing: preferred=redwood-chat-1,fallback=redwood-compact-1; this allows graceful fallback when preferred is busy.
- For private data lanes we recommend pinning tenant to Dedicated capacity in config to avoid cross-tenant slowdowns.

3) Chat vs completions (request/response schema)-
- Chat API: best for multi-turn state where you want system/user/assistant roles preserved and streaming token-level deltas. Typical body (JSON):

  {
    "model": "redwood-chat-1",
    "messages": [ {"role":"system","content":"You are a data assistant."}, {"role":"user","content":"Show me the top 5 customers by ARR"} ],
    "max_tokens": 512,
    "temperature": 0.0,
    "stop": ["\n\n"],
    "stream": false
  }

- Completions API (single prompt): better for short single-shot tasks or when you need a simple prompt->result mapping. Body example:

  {
    "model": "redwood-completions-1",
    "prompt": "Generate a JSON table for top 5 customers by ARR",
    "max_tokens": 256,
    "temperature": 0.0
  }

- Token accounting: tokens are measured on the request + response. For chat, the message history is tokenized and counts toward the request tokens. That means you should trim context or use a KV cache for long histories. max_tokens applies to the response only; the request tokens + max_tokens approximate total token usage.

4) Stop sequences and streaming semantics-
- Streaming (SSE chunks) sends partial tokens/packets as they are generated. If you set stop sequences, the stream will emit the final chunk that contains the stop token and then a final event marking completion. If you need well-formed intermediate structured chunks, we recommend emitting partial records separated by a safe delimiter (e.g., "<ROW_BOUNDARY>") which your client can parse incrementally.
- Caveat: schema validation should be applied on the server once the final response arrives because partial streaming chunks may not be syntactically valid JSON until the end. If you must surface partial rows to the UI, consider streaming CSV/line-delimited JSON rows that can be validated per-line.

5) Structured output & tool calling-
- For deterministic JSON tables, use a two-level approach: 1) instruct the model with a strict schema and an "output_schema" field in the prompt; 2) post-validate using a lightweight JSON schema (we can run this in a Redwood middleware). If the model emits unknown fields, policy is to either drop them or fail the response depending on strictness.
- Tool calling: Redwood supports structured tool calls via our "tools" parameter — you can register a lookup tool that returns canonical results (e.g., product_catalog.lookup(id)). The model returns a tool call object; your runtime executes the tool and feeds back the structured result. This avoids hallucinated lookups.

6) Embeddings and reranker pattern-
- Recommended pipeline for search-with-rerank:
  1) Embed query with our embeddings endpoint (vector dim 1536).
  2) ANN lookup for top 200 candidates (fast recall).
  3) Rerank top 20 with a cross-encoder or a lightweight LLM prompt that scores candidate passages (cheaper to rerank fewer items).

- Note on cost: embedding is relatively cheap per call; reranking with an LLM costs more per-pass. We typically recommend a recall-heavy first stage + narrow rerank.

7) Tokenization and max_tokens practical note-
- Tokenization differences (BPE variants) mean an English sentence typically ~0.8–1.2 tokens per word. Always leave headroom for the model response when setting max_tokens: if you need a 300-token response and you send a 2,000-token context, total tokens may impact latency and cost.
- We can provide a small token-estimation helper in the SDK that approximates request tokens before sending.

Example minimal Chat request with structured JSON output request (non-streaming):

  POST /v1/chat/completions
  Authorization: Bearer <short-lived-key>
  Content-Type: application/json

  {
    "model": "redwood-chat-1",
    "messages": [
      {"role":"system","content":"You are a JSON table generator. Always return valid JSON that conforms to 'schema' field."},
      {"role":"user","content":"Return a JSON array of top 3 customers by revenue with columns [id, name, revenue_usd]."}
    ],
    "output_schema": {"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"id":{"type":"string"},"name":{"type":"string"},"revenue_usd":{"type":"number"}},"required":["id","name","revenue_usd"]}},
    "max_tokens": 300
  }

If the model returns extra fields we advise post-validate and either drop or reject (we can set a strict mode flag in the request).

Attachments / extras: I attached a short code snippet to the drive link in the HubSpot note.

If you'd like, we can run a small PoC where we return line-delimited JSON rows streaming to your UI (gives progressive UX and per-line validation).

I'll be on the deep-dive Wed 3/3 10:00–11:00 PT if that works. Marissa, feel free to schedule.

—Dev Patel
Senior Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference

- The token-exchange flow looks ideal. Can you send the exact exchange endpoint and expected payload so our infra can prototype?
- For streaming line-delimited JSON rows: we'll take that PoC. Would you prefer we start with synchronous streaming of low-volume queries before testing higher throughput?

Let's schedule Wed 3/10 10:00 PT for the PoC kickoff (Dev, Karthik, Laura + our infra). If you can drop the small token-exchange example and a skeleton of the stream consumer client (JS), that would speed things up.

Thanks — Alex
